# Scrollbar

## How To Build

A Scrollbar should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A Scrollbar should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [Theme](../../theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

A permanent scrollbar for any list that scrolls, laid out as a narrow column of its own beside the list rather than over it.

## Description

A narrow column along the right of the list, always shown, whether or not the list has anything to scroll. It is the list's only scrollbar: no scrollbar is laid over the list, or appears only while hovering or scrolling.

## Surface

Every scrollbar is this one, wherever it is. It has no background of its own: the column takes the colour of the surface it sits on, so on the file tree it is the tree's colour, and on a panel's body the body's. Nothing in it is a colour of its own; its border, buttons, thumb, the thumb's ends, the arrows, and the lightening of the thumb and buttons are all white or black laid over that surface, so the scrollbar looks the same on any of them.
The strengths given here are dark mode's. Light mode takes the same steps, its raised parts lighter than the surface as in dark mode: the border, buttons, and thumb are white laid about a third of the way over the surface, the thumb's ends about a sixth, and the thumb and buttons lighten with white laid a fifth of the way while hovered and two fifths while pressed or dragged. Its arrows are darker than the buttons rather than lighter, black laid about a third of the way over them, since white would all but vanish on a light surface.

## Buttons

A square button at the top of the column scrolls the list up a little, and a square button at the bottom scrolls it down a little. The column is 18 pixels wide, and each button is 17 pixels tall, as wide as the column. A button is raised over the surface just as the thumb is, #222222 on #111111 in dark mode, with no bevel, border, or line of its own. It shows a small solid arrow, pointing up or down, 6 pixels wide and 4 tall, centred across it, 7 pixels from its top pointing up and from its bottom pointing down, drawn crisp on whole pixels rather than smoothed, in a faint grey, #4d4d4d on the button's #222222 in dark mode, white laid about a fifth of the way over the button. It lightens as the thumb does: a step while the pointer is over it, and another while pressed with the pointer still over it, across its whole face.

## Track

Between the buttons runs the track, from just beneath the top button to just above the bottom one. The track has no fill: it is the surface it sits on, #111111 on the file tree in dark mode. The whole column is bordered by a line a pixel wide down both its sides, in the buttons' and thumb's colour, #222222 in dark mode, so the border runs straight into the buttons at the top and bottom and the column reads as one raised outline around the track. No line runs across the column, and nothing in it is drawn in the theme's border colour.
The track holds a thumb as tall as the share of the list in view, and never too short to grab, placed as far down the track as the list is scrolled. The thumb is a plain rectangle, as wide as the column, the border and all, with no rounded corners and no bevel, raised over the surface, #222222 on #111111 in dark mode, white laid about 7% of the way over it, so it is brighter than the track. Its top and bottom ends each have a single row of pixels, between the borders, half way between the track and the thumb, #191919 in dark mode, softening where the track meets it. It lightens a step while the pointer is over it, as white laid over it, and another step while it is being dragged, white laid about 3.5% and 7% of the way over it in dark mode, and goes back as soon as neither is true. Nothing in the column lightens while something else, like a sidebar's edge, is being dragged across it. With nothing to scroll, the thumb fills the track.
Pressing the thumb and dragging scrolls the list with it for as long as the button is held, even once the pointer leaves the column, and pressing the track elsewhere moves the thumb there, from where it can be dragged straight away. Where a resize edge beside the list overlaps the column, a press goes to whichever of the two has the smaller hit area, as the main window says.

## Steadiness

The thumb never jumps. Its size and place always reflect the whole list's real height, including a list that only draws the rows in view: every row is measured, even those never scrolled into view, so the thumb doesn't grow, shrink, or leap as rows come into view. A row that arrives, or changes, while out of view counts at its height as soon as it does, and after the list's width changes, rewrapping its rows, the height is known in full again by the next frame. Only what has changed is measured again, so a long list stays as quick to scroll and to add to as one that measures only what is in view; only a change of width measures every row again.
A row's height is the same measured out of view as drawn in it. Text in a row, such as a reply's markdown, is parsed once and kept for as long as the app runs, not only while its row is drawn, so a row scrolled away and back is never parsed again, nor shorter for a moment while it is. Long text is parsed in the background, so a row holding it may first measure short: while it parses, its row is measured again every fraction of a second, for a few seconds at most, so the height is right as soon as the parse lands, whether or not the row is in view. Dragging the thumb, it stays under the pointer the whole way, rows coming into view or not.

## Lock To Bottom

A list that keeps receiving output, like a task's, adds one more square button, drawn as the others are, below the others, with a pixel of the surface between it and the down button, which the column's border runs down both sides of, that locks the scroll to the bottom. Its arrow is the down arrow with a short bar beneath it, the same 6 pixels wide. While it is locked, the button shows as selected, lightened as a pressed button is whether or not the pointer is over it, and the list stays scrolled to the bottom as output arrives. Pressing it again unlocks it. Its tooltip says which it will do.

### Lock Pulse

Whenever the scroll becomes locked, whether by pressing the button or by scrolling to the bottom by hand, a glowing pulse emanates from the lock button once, to confirm it. It is a single, brief confirmation in the manner of Apple's own, not a repeating pulse, which would suggest something still going on.
The pulse is in the theme's focus ring colour. A soft, blurred glow blooms around the button, quickly, and fades away. At the same time two thin rings ripple out from the button's centre, the second a moment after the first, each starting as a circle the size of the button and growing to nearly three times that, easing out so it slows as it spreads, thinning and fading to nothing as it goes. All of it is over in under a second. It is drawn over whatever is beside the column, but never takes the mouse.
A list that shows already locked doesn't pulse, and unlocking the scroll while it pulses stops the pulse straight away.

Scrolling the list by hand locks and unlocks it as well: scrolling with the mouse wheel or trackpad over the list, pressing the column's up or down button, or pressing or dragging its thumb. Scrolled by hand to the bottom, the scroll locks there, just as if the button had been pressed. Scrolled by hand away from the bottom while it is locked, the lock breaks straight away, leaving the list wherever it was scrolled to. A list with nothing to scroll keeps its lock as it is. The button stays the way to lock or unlock it wherever the list is: pressing it to lock scrolls the list to the bottom, and pressing it to unlock leaves the list unlocked until it is next scrolled to the bottom by hand.
17:The tab is one scrolling column, with a [Scrollbar](../../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar), read top to bottom as a timeline, in three groups, each headed by a small muted label with its count: "Previous", every task that has run, oldest at the top, as the [PromptEditor](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s previous tasks are, with their filters and batch actions along the group's heading; "Running", every task under way, in either lane; and "Queued", the queue, in its order, as the [QueueList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list) says, reordered by dragging, its auto-send switch and "Send next" button along its heading. It never scrolls with the list, never appears only while hovering or scrolling, and is never laid over the rows. The headings, pinned or in place, the day dividers, and every row end at the column's left edge, never running beneath it, so the column takes the same 18 pixels of width from all of them and their right-hand parts, the times and the headings' controls, line up against it. 37:The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.

At the same time two thin rings ripple out from the button's centre, the second a moment after the first, each starting as a circle the size of the button and growing to nearly three times that, easing out so it slows as it spreads, thinning and fading to nothing as it goes. All of it is over in under a second. It is drawn over whatever is beside the column, but never takes the mouse.
A list that shows already locked doesn't pulse, and unlocking the scroll while it pulses stops the pulse straight away.

Scrolling the list by hand locks and unlocks it as well: scrolling with the mouse wheel or trackpad over the list, pressing the column's up or down button, or pressing or dragging its thumb. Scrolled by hand to the bottom, the scroll locks there, just as if the button had been pressed. Scrolled by hand away from the bottom while it is locked, the lock breaks straight away, leaving the list wherever it was scrolled to. A list with nothing to scroll keeps its lock as it is. The button stays the way to lock or unlock it wherever the list is: pressing it to lock scrolls the list to the bottom, and pressing it to unlock leaves the list unlocked until it is next scrolled to the bottom by hand.
17:The tab is one scrolling column, with a [Scrollbar](../../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar), read top to bottom as a timeline, in three groups, each headed by a small muted label with its count: "Previous", every task that has run, oldest at the top, as the [PromptEditor](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s previous tasks are, with their filters and batch actions along the group's heading; "Running", every task under way, in either lane; and "Queued", the queue, in its order, as the [QueueList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list) says, reordered by dragging, its auto-send switch and "Send next" button along its heading. A group with nothing in it shows its heading alone, muted, "No queued prompts" and the like. Each time the tab is shown, it is scrolled so the Running group, or the start of the Queued one when nothing runs, is in view.
19:All three headings are always in view, however far the tab is scrolled, so each section's controls are always in reach. A heading whose section starts above the visible rows is pinned at the top of the tab, and one whose section starts below them is pinned at its bottom, in their order: scrolled down into Running, the Previous heading is pinned at the top, the Running heading beneath it, and the Queued heading at the bottom; scrolled into Queued, Previous and Running are pinned at the top, one beneath the other. A heading never pushes another out of view; they stack, each 28 pixels, so the rows scroll in the space left between the headings pinned above and below. A heading in its place among the rows sits there as any row does, and is pinned only once its place leaves the visible rows. Clicking a pinned heading, anywhere but its chevron and controls, scrolls the list to that section's start; clicking its chevron expands or collapses it, as clicking a heading in its place does.
22:The list's [Scrollbar](../../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) is pinned, as every scrollbar is: a column along the tab's right edge, always shown, whether or not the list has anything to scroll, running the tab's full height, from its top to its bottom, beside the pinned headings as well as the rows. It never scrolls with the list, never appears only while hovering or scrolling, and is never laid over the rows. The headings, pinned or in place, the day dividers, and every row end at the column's left edge, never running beneath it, so the column takes the same 18 pixels of width from all of them and their right-hand parts, the times and the headings' controls, line up against it. Its thumb is sized and placed from the whole list, the rows hidden beneath pinned headings and collapsed sections left out, so scrolling it to its bottom shows the last row whole. It has no lock to the bottom, since the list isn't output that keeps arriving.
27:A day's divider is sticky beneath Previous's own heading: while its tasks are scrolled through, it stays pinned just below that heading, until the next day's divider pushes it out, so the day of the rows in view always shows. Day dividers take the place of the session dividers the previous tasks had; a session that starts a new conversation shows a small muted mark at its first row's right instead, its tooltip saying it started a new conversation.
37:The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
38:A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its selection and highlight kept. A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
39:Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll position is clamped to its ends before a frame is drawn, never drawn past an end and corrected the frame after, and kept in whole device pixels, so a row never shimmers between two places. What lies at an end stays at it: a running row's time ticking, a task finishing, a row added or removed elsewhere in the list, or the tab being resized never makes the rows in view jump and settle. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. The list counts as taller than the tab only once it overflows it by a whole pixel, as the right sidebar's panels do, so a list that fits never scrolls at all.
40:Scrolled to its bottom, the last row shows whole, its bottom edge at the bottom of the tab's visible area, never cut off by even a pixel, and nothing lies beneath it but the list's own bottom padding of 8 pixels. However the tab is resized, by the window, the sidebar's panels, or the sidebar's width, the bottom is worked out anew in that frame, so a list scrolled to its bottom still shows its last row whole.
51:A long prompt is clipped: past 8 lines, as they wrap at the tab's width, the Prompt section shows its first 8 and fades the last of them into the section's background, with a "Read more" link beneath, in the theme's accent, with a down chevron. Clicking into a queued task's prompt to edit it shows it whole, as it is being typed in, and it is clipped again once the task is opened afresh.
